name: THE FIFTY GLAZE TO EAT YOUR BURGER

recipe.history:
Red wine reduction sauces and glazes have a lineage that runs through the heart of French classical cuisine, descending from the ancient technique of reducing wine over heat to concentrate its sugars, acids, and flavor compounds into an intensely flavored liquid. The Romans made defrutum — grape must boiled down to half or a third of its original volume — and used it as both sweetener and condiment. Medieval European cooks employed wine reductions in sauces for roasted meats, a tradition that evolved through the Renaissance into the classical French repertoire, where reductions became the foundation of the great wine-based sauces: bordelaise, made with Bordeaux wine and bone marrow; marchand de vin, the wine merchant's sauce; and the humble but magnificent pan sauce, made by deglazing browned bits from the bottom of a skillet with red wine and reducing them with stock into something profound. A true red wine reduction glaze — reduced until it coats the back of a spoon, shining like lacquer, tasting of concentrated fruit and iron and earth — is one of the most transformative things you can apply to beef.

Glazing in American cooking draws from multiple traditions simultaneously: the lacquered meats of Chinese cuisine, the barbecue glazes of the American South and Midwest, the steakhouse pan sauces of fine-dining culture, and the home cook's habit of finishing a skillet steak with a splash of wine and butter. When all these traditions converge in the burger world, they produce something remarkable: a patty finished with a glossy, clinging red wine reduction glaze that caramelizes at the edges and provides a deeply savory, slightly sweet, wine-dark coating that elevates the entire burger into steakhouse territory. Gastropubs and upscale burger restaurants began offering glazed burgers in the 2010s as part of a broader movement to treat ground beef with the same seriousness accorded to a whole steak.

The first time I made a proper red wine reduction, I used a wine I wouldn't have drunk — a supermarket bottle chosen for its low price and my general disinclination to ruin good wine on a sauce. The sauce tasted terrible. A chef friend told me, with the patience of someone who has said this many times before, that you cannot make a good reduction from a wine you wouldn't drink, because reduction concentrates every quality of the wine — including its flaws. I went back and used a decent Côtes du Rhône, something I'd happily pour in a glass, and the resulting glaze was extraordinary — deep and fruity and savory, with a finish that lingered long after the bite. Wine in cooking is not a place for thrift.

The red wine reduction glaze in this recipe clings to the patty in a thin, lacquered layer, setting slightly as it cools during the three-minute rest. This rest — and the medium-rare internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit at which it is achieved — are both non-negotiable. The glaze needs a warm, juicy, fat-rich patty beneath it: the beef's rendered fat carries the glaze's wine and fruit aromatics across the palate, distributing them evenly through every bite. An overcooked patty is dry and dense, and the glaze merely sits on its surface without integration. Medium rare creates the porous, yielding, juice-releasing texture that allows glaze and beef to become one unified flavor. This is the only way this burger works. Fifty glazes says so.
ingredients: 1 tbsp flaky sea salt for topping
For the red wine reduction glaze:
480ml dry red wine (a Côtes du Rhône, Merlot, or Cabernet Sauvignon you would actually drink)
instructions: 1. Make the red wine reduction glaze: Heat olive oil in a small saucepan over medium heat. Add minced shallot and garlic. Cook, stirring, 3 minutes until soft and translucent. Add tomato paste and stir 1 minute until darkened slightly. Add thyme sprigs and bay leaf. Pour in the red wine and increase heat to medium-high. Simmer, stirring occasionally, until reduced by half, about 15 minutes. Add beef stock and continue simmering until the mixture has reduced to about 160ml and coats the back of a spoon, another 15 to 20 minutes. Strain through a fine-mesh sieve, pressing solids. Return to saucepan. Stir in balsamic vinegar, brown sugar, salt, and pepper. Keep warm over very low heat. Just before using, whisk in 1 tablespoon cold butter for sheen and body.

2. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead on medium 8 minutes. Transfer to oiled bowl, cover, rise 1 to 1.5 hours. Shape into 4 balls, proof on a parchment-lined sheet 45 minutes. Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Bake at 375°F (190°C) 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a rack.
3. Make the herb compound butter: Beat softened butter with thyme, rosemary, garlic, salt, and pepper until fully combined. Roll in plastic wrap into a log and refrigerate until firm.

4. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form each into a patty 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Make a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, garlic powder, and onion powder just before cooking.

5. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip and place a slice of aged Gruyère on each. Cook 2 to 2.5 minutes more until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). In the last 30 seconds of cooking, brush a generous tablespoon of red wine reduction glaze over the top of each patty and cheese — it will sizzle and caramelize at the edges. Remove from heat.
6. Brush a final coat of glaze over each patty immediately after removing from the skillet. Rest patties 3 minutes. The glaze will set into a lacquered, glossy layer.
7. Toast bun cut sides in the residual skillet fat over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds. Place a thin slice of herb compound butter on each toasted bun half and let it melt.
8. Toss watercress with olive oil and a pinch of flaky sea salt.

9. Assemble: Set the glazed, rested patty with melted Gruyère on the buttered bottom bun. Top with a small nest of dressed watercress. Drizzle an additional teaspoon of red wine glaze over the watercress and down the sides of the patty. Finish with flaky sea salt and a final grind of black pepper. Cap with the top bun. Serve immediately.
